content: Hydrotalcite is a layered double hydroxide with the chemical formula Mg6Al2CO3(OH)16·4(H2O). Its name originates from its similarity to talc and its high water content. The structural layers of hydrotalcite can stack in different configurations, resulting in either a 3-layer rhombohedral structure (referred to as the 3R polytype) or a 2-layer hexagonal structure (known as the 2H polytype, previously called manasseite). These two structural forms are often found intergrown with one another. The carbonate anions located between the structural layers of hydrotalcite are only weakly bound, which gives the material its anion exchange properties. This characteristic allows hydrotalcite to exchange its interlayer anions with other anions in its environment. Hydrotalcite was first identified in 1842 in a serpentine-magnesite deposit in Snarum, Modum, Buskerud, Norway. It typically forms as an alteration product in serpentinite and is commonly found in association with minerals such as serpentine, dolomite, and hematite. Hydrotalcite has been investigated for its potential use as a scavenger for iodide ions, particularly for the long-lived radioactive isotope iodine-129 (which has a half-life of 15.7 million years). It has also been studied for its ability to capture other radioactive fission products, such as selenium-79 (half-life of 295,000 years) and technetium-99 (half-life of 211,000 years), which are present in spent nuclear fuel. These studies are particularly relevant for the disposal of nuclear waste under oxidizing conditions, such as those found in volcanic tuff at the Yucca Mountain nuclear waste repository. However, a significant challenge in using hydrotalcite for this purpose is that carbonate ions in its structure readily replace iodide ions, reducing its effectiveness as an iodide scavenger. Additionally, the long-term stability of the material over geological time scales is a critical concern when considering its use for radioactive waste sequestration. Layered double hydroxides, such as hydrotalcite, are well-known for their anion exchange capabilities. Beyond its potential applications in nuclear waste management, hydrotalcite is also commonly used as an antacid in medical and pharmaceutical contexts.
